reason: The text presents Hebrew leaders (Moses, Aaron, Joshua, and Caleb) as advocates for the people, not antagonists. When the Israelites complain and want to stone Joshua and Caleb, these leaders fall on their faces (Moses and Aaron) or argue passionately for faith in God's promise (Joshua and Caleb). Moses actively intercedes with God on behalf of the people, invoking divine mercy. The antagonism flows in the opposite direction—the people complain against their leaders and threaten violence against them. The only antagonistic response toward the people comes from God Himself (who threatens plague and death in the wilderness), not from the earthly Hebrew leaders.
